title: Rachel Zegler, Aaron Sorkin, Bradley Whitford, Diego Rodriguez Announced as Speakers at Variety’s Business of Broadway Breakfast
description: Variety has announced programming for its annual Business of Broadway Breakfast, presented by City National Bank. The program, on Oct. 5 in New York
body:
Variety has announced programming for its annual Business of Broadway Breakfast, presented by City National Bank. The program, on Oct. 5 in New York City, will feature Rachel Zegler, Aaron Sorkin, Bradley Whitford and Diego Rodriguez. The event will be hosted by actor Tom Felton (“Harry Potter and the Cursed Child”), who is reprising his role as Draco Malfoy in the “Harry Potter” series.

	Zegler and Rodriguez will be joined by co-star James Olivas for a keynote conversation about the upcoming, “Evita,” which is set to hit the stage in early 2027. “Evita” tells the story of Eva Perón (Rachel Zegler) and her rise from poverty to become one of the most influential women in Latin America.
	

	Joining Aaron Sorkin and Bradley Whitford for the “A Few Good Men” keynote are Tom Blyth, actor and singer Krysta Rodriguez and six-time Tony Award-winning director Michael Arden. The theater adaptation of Sorkin’s 1992 classic film “A Few Good Men” will be revived on Oct. 8 at Lincoln Center’s Vivian Beaumont Theater in New York City.


	The day’s final keynote will feature the cast and crew of “Dolly: A True Original Musical,”opening at the St. James Theater on Jan. 19, on what would have been Dolly Parton’s 81st birthday. Producer Adam Speers, director Bartlett Sherr and the cast bring Dolly Parton and Maria S. Schlatter’s book to life following Dolly from Tennessee to the bright lights of Hollywood.

	The Producers Panel will feature Amanda Lipitz (“Galileo”), Haley Swindal (“Damn Yankees”), Susan Kelechi Watson (“School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play”) and Brian Lee (“Awake and Sing!” and “Here There Are Blueberries”). The panel will be moderated by Erik Piecuch, Senior VP/team leader of entertainment & sports banking at City National Bank.
	

	Variety will also feature the individuals profiled in its 10 Broadway to Watch list, published on Sept. 30, presented by City National Bank.

	“City National Bank is proud to bring together Broadway’s best and brightest to discuss the forces shaping theater today,” said JaHan Wang, head of Entertainment & Sports Banking. “As the leading bank to Broadway, we look forward to helping the community flourish for years to come.”

	“Theater coverage has been at the heart of Variety since its founding more than 120 years ago, and we are deeply honored to carry that legacy forward,” said Dea Lawrence, publisher and co-president of Variety. “Each year, we are proud to bring the industry together with City National Bank to celebrate the enduring vitality of Broadway and look ahead to the stories, productions, and voices that will shape the season to come.”

	Conversations from the event will be posted on Variety.com and across Variety’s social media accounts after the event.

schema.headline: Rachel Zegler, Aaron Sorkin, Bradley Whitford, Diego Rodriguez Announced as Speakers at Variety’s Business of Broadway Breakfast

title: Dick Guttman, Renowned Hollywood Publicist to Stars Including Barbra Streisand and Clint Eastwood, Dies at 93
description: Dick Guttman, the longtime Hollywood publicity executive and screenwriter who worked with clients including Barbra Streisand, Clint Eastwood and man
body:
Dick Guttman, the longtime Hollywood publicity executive and screenwriter who worked with clients including Barbra Streisand, Clint Eastwood and many more, died Sept. 19 in Los Altos, Calif. He was 93.

	Over his many decades in publicity at Rogers & Cowan and his own firms Guttman and Pam and Guttman Associates, he represented Hollywood notables including Paul Newman, Audrey Hepburn, Natalie Wood, Gene Hackman, Warren Beatty, Elizabeth Taylor, William Shatner and many more. 
	

	Guttman moved to Los Angeles from St. Louis, Missouri, with his family after WWII. As his official biography recounts, he rode L.A. streetcars to wait by the soundstage doors of popular radio dramas, collecting used scripts and autographs. He started out in journalism while still at Fairfax High covering high school sports for the Los Angeles Examiner. 


	While attending UCLA, he worked part-time for Rogers & Cowan PR, then became a unit publicist in Europe, where he worked on films including “Paris Holiday” and “The Key.” He met his wife Gisela while in Paris as unit publicist on Billy Wilder’s “Love in the Afternoon,” and they married in 1956.

	When Guttman returned to Los Angeles, he worked at Rogers & Cowan for more than a decade, representing top actors at the time when actors weren’t under contract to studios and “press agents,” in his preferred terminology, became pivotal to successful careers. 

	He partnered with Jerry Pam in 1971 to form Guttman & Pam, which became one of Hollywood’s top agencies over two decades. Guttman formed his own agency, Guttman Associates, in the early 1990s, repping dozens of top stars as well as promoting films such as “Unforgiven,” “Dirty Harry,” “Bonnie and Clyde,” “The Conversation,” “Kramer vs. Kramer,” “All That Jazz,” “The Year of Living Dangerously,” “The Man Who Would Be King,” “The King’s Speech,” “The Artist,” “Shakespeare in Love and “The English Patient.”
	

	Guttman Associates continues to represent Hollywood talent with Guttman’s colleagues Susan Madore and Rona Menashe overseeing the firm.

	Beyond Hollywood, he repped personalities such as author Sidney Sheldon and astronaut Buzz Aldrin as well as companies including Lucasfilm, Industrial Light & Magic, Sanrio’s introduction of Hello Kitty and more.

	Asked if he knew how many clients he had repped, he once said, “I’ve done the rough math, and my guess is probably 700 clients, and about 200 legends. I have been very blessed.”

	Guttman was also a screenwriter on seven films including 1963’s “Back Door to Hell” with Jack Nicholson and TV movies, including collaborations with director Joseph Sargent on “Passion Flower” and “Ivory Hunters.”

	His 2015 autobiography “Starflacker” recounted numerous stories from his decades of working with Hollywood’s biggest stars. 

	After living for more than 50 years in Malibu, he and Gisela moved to Los Altos last year. 

	He is survived by Gisela, his wife of 70 years, his daughters Danielle Guttman Klein and Monika Guttman Robertson, granddaughters Alyssa Brucculeri and Claire Robertson; great-granddaughter Aria Brucculeri and sister Joan Ostrow. 

	Donations may be made to the Dick Guttman Memorial Fund at the Entertainment Industries Foundation, which supports members of the creative community through a variety of philanthropic efforts, including wildfire relief.

title: Jeffrey Katzenberg Says Hollywood Must Accept AI as a Tool: It ‘Is Not Going Away’
description: Jeffrey Katzenberg, the legendary Hollywood producer and executive, thinks the entertainment industry needs to accept AI if it wants to remain relev
body:
Jeffrey Katzenberg, the legendary Hollywood producer and executive, thinks the entertainment industry needs to accept AI if it wants to remain relevant.

	In a 2,377-word essay posted to X on Wednesday, Katzenberg leaned on his history working through the industry’s various technological changes. He implored his fellow creatives to acknowledge AI as a tool similar to those pioneered by the likes of Thomas Edison and adopted by the likes of Charlie Chaplin.
	

	“Hollywood needs to accept that AI is not going away,” Katzenberg wrote. “The energy they are spending trying to make it disappear is energy they are not spending deciding the terms on which it will exist. And the terms are everything. The north needs something from it that they cannot build and cannot buy: creativity. The kind that takes a blank page and conjures a single right answer where there was none and has held audiences for a century. Without it, the most powerful reasoning engine ever invented will still be missing the only thing that makes a story worth telling.”


	The essay follows the yearslong debate over AI’s place within the creative industry, which has further rankled people after AI company leaders acknowledged the tools may slip out of human control.

	Katzenberg’s WndrCo recently invested in Reactor, a startup that says its platform can produce gen-AI video in real time. About Reactor, he told Variety, “I was incredibly impressed, if not astounded, by just how innovative their approach is to storytelling tools.” Katzenberg also has reportedly discussed creating a new AI video startup with the former head of OpenAI’s now-defunct Sora.
	

	Katzenberg, whose career highlights include serving as the chair of Walt Disney Studios and co-founding DreamWorks, compared the wonder he’s felt from witnessing AI tools in action to how he felt when seeing computer-generated imagery appear — and the initial backlash that followed remained similar. While some CGI was used to enhance traditionally animated films like “The Little Mermaid” and “The Lion King,” he wrote, it was Pixar’s “Toy Story” that showcased how “a fully computer-animated film could carry real emotional weight, that it could make audiences laugh, cry, and believe.” When DreamWorks moved into creating fully CGI-animated films, animators who didn’t adapt to the new tools lost their jobs — but, he wrote, the industry could not simply decide whether the tools should or shouldn’t exist.

	“The tools-versus-no-tools argument is a trap,” he wrote. “First, we must all agree that there should be terms. Then we can have the crucial debate about what fairness requires.”

	Once those terms are decided upon and agreed to by all creative stakeholders, Katzenberg thinks it could lead to a new Hollywood renaissance — though he admitted he didn’t have all the answers. “How we come through this is a choice,” he wrote.

	“As the barriers and the costs come down, more films will get made, not fewer,” he wrote. “Studios will get to take more risks. There will be more seats at the table, and very soon entirely new forms of storytelling … Every time storytelling has met a genuine technological shift, from synchronized sound to color to computer animation, it has redefined the boundaries of the medium and grown larger in the process.”

schema.headline: Jeffrey Katzenberg Says Hollywood Must Accept AI as a Tool: It ‘Is Not Going Away’

title: CNN Chief Says He’s ‘Enthusiastic’ About Staying Under Paramount, but Not Sure He Can
description: CNN‘s top executive told staffers Wednesday that he wants to stay at the news giant, but has little knowledge of what the outlet’s soon-to-be new co
body:
CNN‘s top executive told staffers Wednesday that he wants to stay at the news giant, but has little knowledge of what the outlet’s soon-to-be new corporate parent has in store.

	“I am enthusiastic about staying,” CNN CEO Mark Thompson told employees during a town hall meeting, according to two people with knowledge of his remarks. Even so, he also confided he has no knowledge of how Paramount Skydance, which settled an antitrust lawsuit earlier this week with 12 state attorneys general, wants to proceed once it completes its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
	

	“How Paramount wants to run news” is not known to him at present, he said.


	The meeting was scheduled several days ago and not because of Paramount’s victory this week, according to a person familiar with the matter. CNN declined to make executives available for comment. Thompson also told staffers, in response to a question posed by veteran correspondent John King, that he did not know when a transition might start or when Paramount executives might be seen in CNN’s officers.

	CNN personnel have reason for alarm. Paramount’s management of CBS News has been controversial, and has not been good for the business of the news unit. Changes made under Bari Weiss, installed last year as editor in chief, have brought unnecessary scrutiny to news reports, and anchors have made public entreaties on Instagram when people post notes suggesting that Weiss’ background as a digital entrepreneur and provocative opinion writer have muddied the newsgathering at the network. Tweaks made at “CBS Mornings” and “CBS Evening News” are still too nascent to make final judgement, but both shows continue to lag their rivals in the ratings, with the morning show suffering significant erosion. Weiss’ decision to overhaul “60 Minutes,” widely considered the jewel of CBS and of TV-news overall, has left the venerable newsmagazine open to criticism and backlash.
	

	Thompson cautioned staffers that it was not clear that Paramount intended to merge CNN and CBS News, but had no detail to offer about what next steps might look like under the new owner.

	During his tenure, Thompson has focused on getting CNN content in front of younger viewers and digital audiences.  CNN has been testing new formats with its  “CNN All Access” subscription service, and has seen up and coming personnel  like Abby Phillip and Harry Enten gain some traction. Warner Bros. Discovery projected in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission earlier this year that CNN will generate $600 million in profit in 2026 on $1.8 billion in revenue.

schema.headline: CNN Chief Says He’s ‘Enthusiastic’ About Staying Under Paramount, but Not Sure He Can

title: ‘Man on the Inside’ to End With Season 3 at Netflix
description:
“A Man on the Inside” will end with Season 3 at Netflix, which is now in production. 

	The critically-acclaimed comedy was renewed for a third seas
body:
“A Man on the Inside” will end with Season 3 at Netflix, which is now in production. 

	The critically-acclaimed comedy was renewed for a third season back in March, with Season 2 having debuted in January. The series is shooting its third season in San Francisco, CA. 

	“This series began with a retiree taking a chance at a new life. By answering a help wanted ad and venturing out into the world, Charles Nieuwendyk made his world bigger and proved that life only slows down if you let it,” series creator Mike Schur said. “We are thrilled to be able to conclude his journey with one final chapter, as embodied by the great Ted Danson, who I am legally required to refer to as a ‘National Treasure.’” 
	

	The third season of the show will see Danson return along with Mary Elizabeth Ellis, Lilah Richcreek Estrada, Stephanie Beatriz, Eugene Cordero, Stephen McKinley Henderson, Sally Struthers and Mary Steenburgen. 

	Season 3 has also added eight guest stars, who are: Annette O’Toole (“Superman III,” “IT,” “Virgin River”), Bernadette Peters (“The Good Fight,” “The Debut”), Christopher McDonald (“Hacks,” “Happy Gilmore”), Diedrich Bader (“Lucky Hank,” “Better Things,” “American Housewife”), Jessica St. Clair (“The Studio,” “Space Force,” “Avenue 5”), Nick Offerman (“The Last of Us,” “Margo’s Got Money Troubles,” “Parks and Recreation”), Rachel Dratch (“Saturday Night Live,” “30 Rock,” and “The Rocky Horror Show”), and Stephen Root (“Widow’s Bay,” “Barry”). 

	Full character descriptions for the guest stars can be found below. 

	“A Man on the Inside” is based on the documentary “The Mole Agent.” Schur created the series and serves as an executive producer via Fremulon. Morgan Sackett is also an executive producer via Dunshire Productions along with David Miner of 3 Arts Entertainment, Maite Alberdi and Marcela Santibañez of Micromundo Producciones, and Julie Goldman and Christopher Clements of Motto Pictures. Universal Television is the studio.
	

	Season 3 Guest Stars: 

	Annette O’Toole as Kitt: a fixture in San Francisco high society, and one of Coco’s oldest friends

	Bernadette Peters as Coco Van Beck: the Grand Dame of San Francisco society, who hires Charles to find whoever is trying to sabotage her philanthropic work.

	Christopher McDonald as Leland: a playboy vineyard owner and Coco’s third ex-husband.

	Diedrich Bader as Mark Delaurio: a powerful real estate developer who has clashed with Coco many times in the past.

	Jessica St. Clair as Chloe: a friend of Emily’s (Ellis) who helps her navigate a new phase in parenthood.

	Nick Offerman as Jack Spencer: one of Coco’s employees who takes a special interest in Charles’s investigation.

	Rachel Dratch as Maud: Coco’s harried assistant who sleeps three hours a night and has three phones going at all times.

	Stephen Root as Dave: Charles’s estranged brother, who has some old scores to settle.

schema.headline: ‘Man on the Inside’ to End With Season 3 at Netflix

title: David Ellison Mulls Tapping Elon Musk for Paramount Investment While Closing in on Warner Bros. Takeover: Report
description: David Ellison, seeking fresh capital for a merged Paramount-Warner Bros., is considering reaching out to Elon Musk — the controversial tech mogul wh
body:
David Ellison, seeking fresh capital for a merged Paramount-Warner Bros., is considering reaching out to Elon Musk — the controversial tech mogul who is the world’s richest person — to “become part of a syndicate of equity investors into Paramount,” according to a report by Semafor.

	According to the report, citing anonymous sources, “Musk’s name is one of a number of wealthy individuals that Paramount CEO David Ellison has considered tapping for the syndicate,” but it did not identify others Ellison is supposedly mulling as investment partners. The Semafor report said the amount of Musk’s potential investment in Paramount could not be learned.
	

	Paramount declined to comment. A rep for Musk did not immediately respond to a request for comment.


	Musk, the one-time Trump administration official who leads SpaceX, Tesla and X, among other businesses, had a net worth estimated at about $950 billion as of Wednesday, per Forbes.

	Paramount’s deal to merge with Warner Bros. Discovery is close to the finish line, after the company reached a settlement with 12 state attorneys general to settle their antitrust lawsuit over the pact. The judge in the case has scheduled a hearing Thursday to go over the points of the proposed consent decree; pending the judge’s approval, the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger is expected to close in about two weeks.

	Oracle founder Larry Ellison (David’s father), who is also one of the world’s richest men, has business ties to Musk: Larry Ellison invested $1 billion in Musk’s 2022 deal taking Twitter (since renamed X) private. Larry Ellison also invested in Tesla in 2018, and served on its board for several years.
	

	For Paramount’s WBD deal, valued at $111 billion, Larry Ellison has personally guaranteed $46.7 billion in equity financing. In addition, Paramount has lined up $24 billion in commitments from the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. According to Paramount, the three Middle Eastern funds would own 38.5% of the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. Last week, the FCC approved Paramount’s petition to allow 49.5% of its equity to be held by foreign entities if the Warner Bros. Discovery merger is consummated.

	Among the top-line terms in Paramount’s settlement with the states: Paramount is prohibited from selling the Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots in the state for at least five years, and is obligated to invest at least an additional $300 million on film production in the U.S. annually (for a total of $1.5 billion over five years). The newly merged company also must release at least 30 movies for theatrical distribution in the first two years (something Ellison has repeatedly promised he would do) and at least 32 in years 3-5, with a 45-day window for wide-release films. 

	In addition, under the proposed settlement, the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. also will be subject to monitoring by a “news editorial independence board,” which will establish “guiding editorial and journalism principles for” for CNN and CBS News.

schema.headline: David Ellison Mulls Tapping Elon Musk for Paramount Investment While Closing in on Warner Bros. Takeover: Report

title: Diane Lane Joins Li Jun Li in Hulu Limited Series ‘Victoria’
description:
Diane Lane has joined the upcoming Hulu-Onyx Collective limited series “Victoria,” Variety has learned. 

	The erotic thriller, which was announced
body:
Diane Lane has joined the upcoming Hulu-Onyx Collective limited series “Victoria,” Variety has learned. 

	The erotic thriller, which was announced last week with a series order, will star Li Jun Li as Maxine Tao, who is described as “a brilliant con artist who finds herself in a dark web of power, luxury and the crosshairs of a seductive killer who knows her secrets.”

	Lane joins as Lee Calloway, said to be “a savvy venture capitalist accustomed to getting what she wants and has worked too hard to let anyone stand between her and the win.”
	

	This is the latest in a string of high-profile TV roles Lane has taken on in recent years. She previously appeared in shows like “A Man in Full” and “House of Cards” at Netflix, as well as Season 2 of “Feud” for FX/Hulu and “The Romanoffs” at Amazon. She is primarily known for her roles in films like “Under the Tuscan Sun,” “Unfaithful,” and “Hollywoodland.” Her work in “Unfaithful” earned her both an Academy Award and Golden Globe nominations, while she was also nominated for Golden Globes for “Under the Tuscan Sun” and the TV movie “Cinema Verite.” “Cinema Verite” also earned her an Emmy nomination, as did “Feud,” while Lane was nominated for an Emmy early in her career for the CBS miniseries “Lonesome Dove.” 


	She is repped by CAA, Range, and Weintraub. 

	Christy Hall is the creator, writer, executive producer, and showrunner on “Victoria.” Geeta Vasant Patel will direct the pilot and executive produce. Lilly Burns, Elise Henderson, and Tony Hernandez of Counterpart Studios executive produce, with Li co-producing in addition to starring.

schema.headline: Diane Lane Joins Li Jun Li in Hulu Limited Series ‘Victoria’

title: ‘Conclave’ Director Edward Berger, Matthew Libatique to Be Feted at Evolution Mallorca International Film Festival
description: Oscar-winning Swiss-Austrian director Edward Berger (“Conclave,” “All Quiet on the Western Front”) and American cinematographer Matthew Libatique (“
body:
Oscar-winning Swiss-Austrian director Edward Berger (“Conclave,” “All Quiet on the Western Front”) and American cinematographer Matthew Libatique (“Requiem for a Dream,” “Black Swan”), a triple Oscar nominee,  will receive the top honors at the upcoming Evolution Mallorca International Film Festival. The event, which takes place in the largest of Spain’s Balearic Islands between Oct. 28 and Nov. 4, will also honor veteran German actress Iris Berben (“Triangle of Sadness”).
	

	Berger will receive the Evolution Vision Award, which recognizes narrative excellence reflecting the mission of building bridges between cultures and people. Libatique will receive the Cinematography Icon Award, recognizing artistic and technical excellence in the art of cinematography, while Berben will be honored with the Evolution Icon Award in homage to a performer whose extensive and brilliant career has achieved international acclaim.


	In celebration of Berger, the festival will host a special screening of Cannes Best Director winner “Fatherland,” directed by Paweł Pawlikowski and produced by the “Conclave” director. The screening will be followed by a conversation between Berger and producer Jeanne Tremsal. Earlier this week, it was announced Berger would be reteaming with “The Riders” star Brad Pitt for a long-anticipated “World War Z” sequel.

	Berben will receive the inaugural Evolution Icon Award during the festival’s opening gala on Oct. 28. The festival has praised Berben’s work beyond the screen, especially her tenure as the President of the German Film Academy between 2010 and 2019, where she “helped strengthen the public profile and cultural significance of German cinema.”
	

	As for Libatique, Darren Aronofsky’s frequent collaborator will give an Icon Talk followed by a roundtable discussion on cinematography. Libatique is the fifth recipient of the award dedicated to the craft, with the festival also hosting a Cinematography Focus forum between Oct. 28-30. The forum “reinforces one of Evolution’s key professional platforms, dedicated specifically to the craft, technique, and creation of the cinematic image.”

	Spanish actor and producer Marc Clotet will preside over this year’s jury. The actor’s return to Mallorca has a special significance, given that he was featured in Benito Zambrano’s “The Sleeping Voice,” the opening film of the festival’s inaugural edition in 2012. “I am delighted to serve as jury president for a festival as special to me as the Evolution Film Festival,” Clotet said. “15 years after attending the first edition, being able to contribute my perspective after all these years of experience is a challenge I approach with great respect and excitement.”

	Goya-nominated Clotet has built a career spanning both national and international projects. In 2021, Clotet founded the production company Funicular Films alongside Aina Clotet, Marta Baldó, and Jan Andreu. Through this company, he has spearheaded projects such as the successful series “This Is Not Sweden” and the Cannes Critics’ Week-winning film “Viva,” which played at the major French festival earlier this year.

	The festival also revealed more details of its Made in Baleares section, dedicated to bridging together films from the Balearic Islands. This year, the section will feature 32 projects, including 17 short films, seven feature films, five documentary short films and three student short films. The selection reflects the diversity, professional growth, and rising ambition of the Balearic audiovisual sector. It also reinforces Evolution’s commitment to a program that blends local talent with new voices and established figures from international cinema.

	The festival’s 15th edition will also see the event expand into the municipality of Calvià, which is celebrating its Year of Cinema in 2026. The festival notes the expansion reinforces “its commitment to the audiovisual sector as a cultural, creative, and economic driver, as well as a tool to showcase the region and attract new productions.”
	

	“Celebrating our fifteenth edition is a momentous occasion for Evolution,” said Sandra Lipski, founder and director of the Evolution Mallorca International Film Festival. “We are proud to continue building a platform where international voices and local talent converge. Our new collaboration with Calvià reflects a shared ambition: to create meaningful opportunities for filmmakers, promote Mallorca as an exceptional filming location, and contribute to the growth of the island’s audiovisual community.”

	The Mayor of Calvià has highlighted the significance of the municipality hosting the festival this year, stating that the “arrival of the Evolution festival represents a renewed commitment to cinema as an audiovisual sector that helps reduce seasonality, while also attracting high-quality tourism.”

	The Evolution Mallorca International Film Festival was founded in 2012 to promote Mallorca as a key destination for international film culture. The full program, screening schedules, and upcoming guest announcements will be revealed on Oct. 15.

schema.headline: ‘Conclave’ Director Edward Berger, Matthew Libatique to Be Feted at Evolution Mallorca International Film Festival

title: CNN’s Interactive ‘Office Hours’ Has John Berman Testing New Skills
description: John Berman has done almost everything an anchor can do at CNN. He guides viewers through breaking news during hours of “CNN News Central.” He’s fil
body:
John Berman has done almost everything an anchor can do at CNN. He guides viewers through breaking news during hours of “CNN News Central.” He’s filled in for Anderson Cooper, co-hosted a morning show and is trained to handle CNN’s “Magic Wall” on primary and election nights.

	Now he has a new assignment – but you won’t find it on the traditional CNN schedule


	Berman has been hosting a new CNN program called “Office Hours” that runs weekly on the news giant’s nascent subscription product “CNN All Access.” During “Office Hours,” Berman interacts with subscribers and helps to answer their questions about elections, politics and more. On Wednesday evening, Berman will host this week’s edition of the program alongside Kate Bolduan and Sara Sidner, his “News Central” co-hosts.
	

	“This doesn’t feel like television,” Berman says during a recent interview. “Even though there are cameras rolling.”

	Berman is one of a growing number of traditional news anchors being assigned to new interactive formats that give viewers and subscribers more say over what gets discussed. Across the TV-news sector, there is an emerging focus on letting the people who are tuning in have more say or on hiring people with deep expertise in a certain topic who can help guide news aficionados in a more personal, unvarnished way.

	“You have this great tribe of people” coming to CNN’s digital venues, says Ryan Kadro, senior vice president of content strategy at the Warner Bros. Discovery-backed news unit. “People are watching video, reading all of the articles and want to keep going further.” He adds: “The baseline premise we’ve had for a long time is that we need to engage more directly with people that are coming to us and make talent available.”
	

	CNN also faces competitive pressures. MS NOW has put significant emphasis on giving more access to its anchors and correspondents via interactive video sessions on its new “Membership” subscription product. Even Rachel Maddow and members of “Morning Joe” have committed to weekly hangouts with subscribers. And of course, there are many other digital corners where headline-seekers can talk to one another. 

	“So many of these conversations were done on platforms in other places — in comments, on X,” says Kadro. CNN’s goal was “to take the conversations happening around us and bring it to our ecosystem and make our subscriptions stickier.” CNN has introduced new on-screen elements to some of its TV programs — like a “rail” for text chats from correspondents —  in a bid to keep conversations from moving elsewhere.

	Even so, executives have been methodical, not rushed, about crafting CNN’s new interactive format. CNN did three or four early sessions via Zoom, Kadro says, then sought feedback from attendees. Participation on the first “Office Hours” with Berman was three times what had been expected, Kadro says. From there, the company set about crafting something that would work on its new app.

	The new show puts Berman into situations he might not typically encounter on TV. During one recent “Office Hours” ostensibly focused on the coming midterm elections, the anchor found he kept getting questions and comments about President Trump’s proposal to hand out $5,000 checks to Americans if Republicans emerged victorious. “On TV, we talked about it and it went away,” he says, but “not for the people we were talking to.” With that in mind, Berman knew he could turn the interactions into a conversation the next time he was anchoring on TV. “I was getting direct feedback at night and turning it around in the morning.”

	Now that Paramount Skydance has prevailed in its bid to take over CNN’s parent, there is certain to be new scrutiny on what elements of CNN’s current business plan new managers wish to keep. For a TV veteran like Berman, there is, for now, a chance to pivot when it comes to facilitating new kinds of interactions with news viewers. “I’m trying to respond to the people who are viewing it,” Berman notes. “I don’t have control, and I don’t mind that.”

schema.headline: CNN’s Interactive ‘Office Hours’ Has John Berman Testing New Skills

title: Power at Any Age: Gloria Reuben Urges Menopausal Women to Advocate for Their Health
description: Throughout her illustrious life and career, Gloria Reuben has shared her story through music and acting. She started learning classical piano when s
body:
Throughout her illustrious life and career, Gloria Reuben has shared her story through music and acting. She started learning classical piano when she was a young girl and was the lead singer of a rock band as a teenager. Then in her early 20s, Reuben moved from Toronto to Los Angeles, where she waited tables at a restaurant and took acting classes before booking her first big break, a TV commercial. Soon after, she made the jump from full-time waitress to working actress in order to pursue her creative passions. “You made the right decision. Keep the faith,” she told herself at the time.
	

	These days, the veteran entertainer is starring in multiple TV series, shooting films and regularly performing jazz. Creative expression — specifically music, what she calls the “enduring factor” in her life — has carried her through everything she’s achieved and conquered, and how she’s navigated the world of show business for decades.

	Now, the actress and musician is sharing the latest chapter of her story. 

	For several years, Reuben was navigating a force shaping nearly every part of her daily life – menopause, specifically, hot flashes due to menopause.

	Vacation plans and long flights required strategizing and prepping to manage sudden waves of heat. At work, wardrobe fittings suddenly meant second-guessing fabrics and layers in case of hot flashes on and off camera. Then, on set, she felt disconnected from her scene partners, which forced her to be in her head instead of in the present moment. “I felt like I didn’t know my body anymore,” she shares. “Like my body was a stranger. It was very unsettling.” For years, Reuben was navigating moderate to severe hot flashes due to menopause, both day and night, with constant uncertainty of when the next one might strike.
	

	For much of women’s lives, change is something they learn to navigate. From puberty and first heartbreak to career pivots and, for some, motherhood, women are thrown into an endless evolution of identity that comes with simply being alive.

	Then comes menopause.



	

					OK McCausland for Variety
	



	It’s a transition that remains one of the most misunderstood and underdiscussed health topics, yet all women who reach midlife will experience menopause. Menopause is a natural occurrence in a woman’s life and is defined by 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period. Too often, menopause — including hot flashes — has been framed as something women are expected to endure and struggle with, as though aging itself is something to apologize for. In fact, hot flashes are one of the most commonly reported symptoms of menopause.

	Nearly half of women going through menopause may experience moderate to severe hot flashes, and these symptoms may last 10 or more years for some. Menopausal hot flashes and night sweats disproportionately impact women of color, with Black and Hispanic women experiencing more frequent and bothersome hot flashes due to menopause.

	The increasing frequency and unpredictability of Reuben’s hot flashes, including sleep disruptions from nighttime hot flashes, took a toll. “When the natural phase of a woman’s body changes into the phase of menopause, for me, personally, it definitely brought a lot of things into question,” she shares, alluding to the mental toll and fears of a hot flash “erupting” during a day on set or an evening out. “It’s very challenging on all fronts, especially if a woman is being silent about it or struggling with it on her own… I carried, unknowingly I think, a great deal of shame around it and embarrassment,” she says. “That was very difficult.”



	

					OK McCausland for Variety
	



	There’s no one-size-fits-all approach to managing moderate to severe hot flashes due to menopause. But there are treatment options available. One option is VEOZAH, the #1 prescribed hormone-free treatment FDA-approved for moderate to severe hot flashes due to menopause.* VEOZAH blocks the binding of NKB, a brain chemical known to trigger hot flashes during menopause, in the brain’s temperature control center. VEOZAH is not a hormone. It’s proven to reduce the number and severity of hot flashes, day and night, based on clinical studies measuring efficacy over 24 hours at four and 12 weeks. For some women, it can start working as early as one week, but results may vary from person to person and women should speak with their doctor about what this may mean for them.
	

	It’s important for people to know that VEOZAH can cause serious side effects, including liver problems. Expect blood tests before and during treatment. Stop VEOZAH and call your doctor if you have signs or symptoms of liver problems, like feeling more tired, decreased appetite, nausea, vomiting, itching, yellowing of eyes or skin, pale stool, dark urine or stomach pain. Keep reading for additional Important Safety Information, including BOXED WARNING.

	Reuben first heard about VEOZAH when she saw a television commercial for the treatment and later consulted with her doctor about her menopausal hot flashes. “I was looking for a hormone-free and FDA-approved option,” she says. For Reuben, conversations with her doctor and advocating for her own health led to her choosing VEOZAH as the treatment option for her moderate to severe hot flashes due to menopause. “We talked about treatment options, including the possible benefits and possible side effects. Before starting VEOZAH, my doctor did a blood test to check my liver, and since I’ve been taking VEOZAH, my doctor has done follow-up liver blood testing,” she recalls. “I got my prescription a few days later, and in about a week there was a decrease in my menopausal hot flashes, both day and night.” Individual results may vary and women should speak with their doctor about what this may mean for them.

	The menopause advocate adds, “VEOZAH has worked well for me as a treatment for my moderate to severe hot flashes due to menopause. I’m not constantly wondering when the next hot flash will happen.”



	

					OK McCausland for Variety
	



	For Reuben, as her hot flashes became less frequent, so did the worry that came with anticipating when the next one might strike. “Instead of planning my day, and night, around my hot flashes, I can focus more on the things that matter most to me,” she shares.

	Don’t use VEOZAH if you have cirrhosis, severe kidney problems, kidney failure or take CYP1A2 inhibitors. Keep reading for additional Important Safety Information, including BOXED WARNING.

	“I’m always collaborating and always keeping in touch with my health care provider,” Reuben shares.



	

					OK McCausland for Variety
	



	Beyond the physical symptoms, Reuben says menopause prompted an unexpected reckoning. She started to confront bigger questions about what this next stage of life could look like. Rather than viewing menopause as an ending, she began reframing it as an invitation to advocate for herself physically and emotionally — a perspective that would ultimately shape the way she approached her overall health. “It feels good to be reconnected,” she says of her mind and body.
	

	Reflecting on her menopausal experiences, Reuben says advocating for herself and her health “in every single way” allowed her to “participate in my own healing process. I found a way to reframe every area of my life. It’s not just a new chapter, it’s a new volume.”

	One of the biggest lessons menopause taught Reuben is that strength doesn’t always mean handling everything alone. She hopes more women feel comfortable asking questions and leaning on trusted health care providers.

	“I experienced that ‘you have to do it all. You have to be a superwoman. You have to just handle it.’ Yes, sometimes, and sometimes you have to ask for help,” Reuben says. “Oftentimes in my life it’s been, ‘Oh no, I got this. Oh, I can handle this.’ The asking for help, asking questions and being open to communicate about what’s really going on is key for all of us. In particular, when a woman’s body is changing and there are a lot of questions to ask. It’s a very unknown territory because each body is different. Each woman’s experience is going to be different. However, you don’t have to do it alone. The first step is communicating with your health care provider. Learning about the science of what’s going on, listening to your body and communication.”



	

					OK McCausland for Variety
	



	Power does not expire with age. Knowledge and shared stories empower women at any age to transform uncertainty into actionable clarity. 

	“Unexpectedly for me, this time of my life has been a really joyful time of freedom that I didn’t anticipate and there’s an openness that I definitely didn’t anticipate,” she says. 

	Joyful freedom has led Reuben to pursue her creative passions with renewed exuberance and fewer struggles. Reuben wrote her first book, “My Brothers’ Keeper: Two Brothers. Loved. and Lost.,” and recently wrote her first play. She’s regularly journaling, working on TV and film sets, creating playlists for each character she portrays, performing on stages and pulling inspiration from her own life for artistic endeavors.

	Music is still her longstanding throughline, healing force and inspiration. She’s also inspiring others. 

	“I’d like women who are going through menopause and experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes, day and night, to know about the treatment option that worked for me,” she says. “I’d encourage them to speak to their health care provider, discuss what they’re feeling and the possible treatment options for them. They don’t have to suffer in silence. They don’t have to grin and bear it. They don’t have to do it alone.”
	

	To learn more, visit VEOZAH.com 

	*IQVIA TRx data from May 2023 to June 2026


	What is VEOZAH™ (fezolinetant)? VEOZAH is a prescription medicine used to reduce moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms due to menopause. VEOZAH is not a hormone. Vasomotor symptoms are the feelings of warmth in the face, neck, and chest, or sudden intense feelings of heat and sweating (“hot flashes” or “hot flushes”).

	IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION

	What is the most important information I should know about VEOZAH? VEOZAH can cause serious side effects, including:


Liver Problems. Your healthcare provider will do a blood test to check your liver before you start taking VEOZAH. Your healthcare provider will also do this blood test monthly for the first 3 months, at month 6, and month 9 after you start taking VEOZAH or if you have signs or symptoms that suggest liver problems. If your liver blood test values are elevated, your healthcare provider may advise you to stop treatment or request additional liver blood tests.



	Stop VEOZAH right away and call your healthcare provider if you have the following signs or symptoms of liver problems:


feeling more tired than you do usually 
decreased appetite 
nausea 
vomiting 
itching 
yellowing of the eyes or skin (jaundice) 
pale feces 
dark urine 
pain in the stomach (abdomen)



	Do not use VEOZAH if you:


have cirrhosis. 
have severe kidney problems or kidney failure. 
are taking certain medicines called CYP1A2 inhibitors. Ask your healthcare provider if you are not sure.



	Before you use VEOZAH, tell your healthcare provider about all of your medical conditions, including if you:


have liver disease or problems. 
have kidney problems. 
have any medical conditions that may become worse while you are using VEOZAH.



	Tell your healthcare provider about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements. VEOZAH may affect the way other medicines work, and other medicines may affect how VEOZAH works.

	The most common side effects of VEOZAH include:


stomach (abdominal) pain 
diarrhea 
difficulty sleeping (insomnia) 
back pain 
hot flashes or hot flushes



	These are not all the possible side effects of VEOZAH. Tell your healthcare provider if you have any side effect that bothers you or does not go away.

	Call your healthcare provider for medical advice about side effects. You are encouraged to report negative side effects of prescription drugs to the FDA. Visit www.fda.gov/medwatch or call 1-800- FDA-1088. 

	Please see full Prescribing Information and Patient Information, including BOXED WARNING at VEOZAH.com.

title: Model Found Stabbed to Death in Ex's Car After She Told Mom He Was At Her House
description:
Brazilian Model
                          Found Stabbed to Death in Ex's Car
body:
Brazilian Model
                          Found Stabbed to Death in Ex's Car
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 23, 2026
                            10:51 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 23, 2026
                                11:33 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            A Brazilian model was found stabbed to death in her ex's car ... after she'd texted her mom that he'd turned up at her home.
      
    
            Larissa Brito's body was reportedly found during a random customs check of her ex Mathieu's car in Brignoles, France.
      
    
            A local outlet says she was hidden under plastic bags in the backseat ... and her 29-year-old ex was arrested.
      

            According to reports, Larissa moved to France a few years back and dated Mathieu for about five months.
      
    
            She reportedly broke up with him when she learned he was allegedly involved with organized crime and had previous convictions.
      
    
            The reports say Larissa moved to Nice because Mathieu began stalking her. Just hours before her body was found, the model reportedly texted her mom that Mathieu had shown up at her home, saying ... "Mathieu is here."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            According to a Brazilian outlet, Larissa's mom called Mathieu, who claimed her daughter was sleeping. When she threatened to call the cops, Mathieu blocked her number.
      
    
            It's unclear when exactly Larissa was killed, and her autopsy is scheduled for next week. Her mom is trying to have her body returned to Brazil.
      
    
            Larissa was 25.
      
    
            RIP

title: Harvey Weinstein Sentenced to 15 Years in Prison After NYC Retrial
description:
Harvey Weinstein
                          Sentenced to 15 Years in NYC ...
body:
Harvey Weinstein
                          Sentenced to 15 Years in NYC ...
                          After Retrial Put Case in Doubt
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 23, 2026
                            9:16 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison after a jury convicted him again during his retrial in New York last year.
      
    
            The disgraced movie producer was sentenced in a Manhattan courthouse on Wednesday, more than a year after a jury found him guilty of a first-degree criminal sexual act for sexually assaulting former “Project Runway” production assistant Miriam Haley.
      
    
            Miriam appeared in court as well and read a victim impact statement for the record ... saying Weinstein's actions gave her a life sentence -- because it seriously destroyed her sense of safety.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Weinstein also spoke in court ... where he apologized for mistakes he's made in the past -- but insists he never violently attacked anyone.
      
    
            Judge Curtis Farber -- who sentenced Weinstein -- bashed the 74-year-old ... telling him, “You took what you wanted by force, and you have never accepted responsibility."
      
    
            Manhattan DA Alvin Bragg said after the sentencing ... “Today was about the survivors. Ms. Haley, her remarks were powerful, moving, and eloquent. I thank her first and foremost, and all of the survivors who came to lend their support. I’m moved, as we should all be moved, by their courage and their steadfastness through what has obviously been a challenging process.”
      
    
            Weinstein was initially convicted in 2020 of third-degree rape involving Jessica Mann and first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley, and he was sentenced to 23 years.
      
    
            However, the New York State Appeals Court overturned the conviction in 2024, and Weinstein was retried last year. He was still found guilty of first-degree criminal sexual act ... though the jury couldn't come to a consensus on the third-degree rape count.
      
    
            He's also been convicted of rape and sexual assault in California ... but an appeals court vacated his original sentence. He has not yet been resentenced.
      
    
            While originally on Rikers Island, Weinstein is now in the medical unit for jail inmates at Bellevue Hospital due to ongoing health issues.

title: College Wrestler Fell to His Death at Yosemite National Park
description:
California College Wrestler
                          Falls to His Death at Yosemite
body:
California College Wrestler
                          Falls to His Death at Yosemite
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 23, 2026
                            12:14 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A California college wrestler is dead after he fell near Illilouette Falls at Yosemite National Park.
      
    
            Santa Rosa Junior College Coach Fred Duerr confirmed that wrestler Ryan George died over the weekend ... according to multiple reports.
      
    
            Duerr said ... "If you knew Ryan, you know he was one of the most genuine, positive people you could ever meet. He had this way of lighting up a room, making you feel welcome, and bringing out the best in everyone around him."
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The coach recalled that Ryan was "always smiling, always encouraging, always full of life."
      
    
            Ryan's college coach said he "was an amazing leader and wrestler, but more than that, he was an amazing human."
      
    
            Duerr added ... "We love you and we will miss you so much, Ryan. Thank you for everything you gave us."
      
    
            Ryan reportedly competed in the Dave Pacheco Invitational in Sacramento just days before his tragic death.
      
    
            He was 19.
      
    
            RIP
